entries.abstract: In the visible game of cops and robber on a finite connected undirected graph, let c(G) be the least number of cops who can force capture. A multiscale pursuit argument gives c(G) ≤ n^(2/3 + e(n)) on every graph of order n, with one positive function e(n) tending to zero uniformly over the choice of graph. In particular, there are constants δ > 0 and C > 0 such that c(G) ≤ C n^(1 − δ) for every such graph, as asserted by the weak Meyniel conjecture. The repository also contains a separate formalization of the shorter proof giving c(G) ≤ 31 n^(3/4) log(2n).
entries.title: The weak Meyniel conjecture and a two-thirds exponent for the cop number

entries.abstract: With logarithms to base two, let m(n) be the least m for which some n-vertex graph contains both a clique and an independent set of order ⌈log n⌉ in every set of m vertices. In 1991 Erdős asked whether m(n) ≤ ⌈(log n)^3⌉ for arbitrarily large n. We answer this question negatively by proving that m(n) > (log n)^(7/2)/(log log n)^24 for all sufficiently large n, improving a bound of Alon and Sudakov (2007). We also give a simple construction that improves the upper bound of Alon, Bucić and Sudakov (2021) from 2^(2^((log log n)^(1/2+o(1)))) to 2^((9/2+o(1))(log log n)^2). Both bounds are formalized in Lean 4.
entries.title: Improved bounds for locally Ramsey graphs

entries.abstract: Aristotle (De Caelo III.8) claimed that regular tetrahedra fill space; the refutation is credited to Regiomontanus, and the history is told by Lagarias and Zong (2012). This entry proves in Lean that there is no tiling of 3-space by similar copies of the regular tetrahedron, and the same for the regular octahedron, dodecahedron and icosahedron. Tiles are convex polytopes, need not meet face to face, and may each have their own scale. With helper tiles whose dihedral angles are nonnegative rational multiples of pi (cubes, for instance), no tile is a copy of the polyhedron; in a tiling by the five Platonic polyhedra and such helpers, no tile is a dodecahedron or an icosahedron. The proof reads each dihedral angle from the set, uses that the angles round an edge add up to 2 pi (each a dihedral angle, pi or 2 pi), and that pi, arctan of the golden ratio, arccos(1/sqrt 6) and arccos(sqrt(2/3)) are linearly independent over Q, by Niven's theorem (Mathlib niven) and a field argument. Tilings are locally finite by definition, and each polyhedron is one fixed set in exact coordinates. None of these theorems is new; the entry gives their Lean proofs. Audience: researchers on tilings and polyhedra, and Mathlib contributors.
entries.title: Aristotle's Error, Machine-Checked: Regular Tetrahedra Do Not Fill Space

entries.abstract: In the shifted Antihydra recurrence on natural-number pairs, each successful round sends x to floor(3x/2). Even x earns two units of credit. Odd x spends one unit and halts at zero credit. From (8, 0), no semilinear set containing the seed admits a successful successor within the set for every member. The proof also gives a quantitative horizontal-ray bound and the Presburger-definable corollary. The seed's halting behavior is open in this work, and priority is unclaimed.
entries.title: Antihydra has no semilinear inductive safety invariant

entries.abstract: For every real number ξ > 0, the sequence of integer parts ⌊ξ(7/5)^n⌋, n = 0, 1, 2, …, contains infinitely many composite terms. The Lean proof establishes the stronger statement that infinitely many terms share a nontrivial divisor with 4290 = 2·3·5·11·13, by a finite graph certificate: an orbit avoiding these five primes would give an infinite walk in a finite labelled graph whose vertices record a residue modulo 4290 and a cell of the fractional part, refined in four stages from 32 to 2048 cells, and every cyclic strongly connected component of that graph is excluded by a rank and phase certificate together with an elementary lemma that the carry sequence of such an orbit is not eventually periodic. The finite certificate is checked inside the Lean kernel (`decide +kernel`); no `native_decide` and no axioms beyond `propext`, `Classical.choice` and `Quot.sound` are used.
entries.title: Infinitely many composite terms in the floor sequence of ξ(7/5)^n

entries.abstract: A point of the square lattice has eight neighbours. Let delta(n) be the greatest upper density of a set S such that every point of S has at most n neighbours in S. Elkies introduced delta(n) and proved delta(3) = 1/2, which implies that no still Life of Conway's Game of Life has density greater than 1/2 (the still-Life conjecture). Ionascu, Pritikin and Wright studied the limit of the densities of n-dependent sets in finite kings graphs and conjectured the values 3/5 and 9/13 for n = 4 and n = 5, with upper bounds 0.608956 and 0.693943. This project proves delta(3) = 1/2, the same for still Lifes, delta(4) = 3/5 and delta(5) = 9/13, each as the greatest element of the set of upper densities. For n = 3 the proof is the one of Chu and Stuckey. For n = 4 and n = 5 the upper bound is an inequality in windows of four or three rows of five cells with two functions whose contributions telescope; the functions are given by tables, and the kernel checks the inequality in every window. Elkies reports that M. Moore announced delta(5) = 9/13 in 1995. We have not found a published proof for n = 4 or n = 5; whether these two results are new is unknown to us.
entries.title: The greatest density of a set in the square lattice whose points have at most three, four or five neighbours

entries.abstract: DICTO's paper "Fair Dice — The Aequi: Enumerating the Innumerable" (Zenodo, 2026) proves, as its Theorem A (a), that a set of N distinct face directions, not all in one closed hemisphere, carries a die that is fair about the origin (every face seen from the origin under the solid angle 4 pi / N) exactly when the directions satisfy Alexandrov's condition for equal masses, and that the die is then unique up to scale. The proof passes to the polar polytope, whose corners lie on the face directions; the paper's Lemma 1 shows that the solid angle of a face equals the integral Gauss curvature of the polar polytope at the matching corner, so Theorem A (a) is Alexandrov's theorem on prescribed integral curvature (Alexandrov 1942, in the polytope case proved by Oliker 2007 and Bertrand 2016) for equal curvatures. This entry proves in Lean the polyhedral Alexandrov theorem with the condition stated over sets of rays (existence if and only if the curvatures sum to 4 pi and Alexandrov's condition holds for every nonempty proper set of the rays; uniqueness up to scaling about the origin); the equivalence of this form with the textbook form over spherically convex sets is not formalized. Curvature and solid angle are each defined as three times a volume inside the unit ball (the normal cone, or the cone through a face), which equals the corresponding area on the unit sphere. The entry also proves Lemma 1 (the polar identity) and Theorem A (a) (existence and uniqueness of the fair die). Existence follows Oliker's variational route: a maximizer of his functional exists by continuity and coercivity, and at a maximizer every corner has the prescribed curvature. Uniqueness is by the maximum principle. Not formalized: Theorem A (b) (the symmetry group of the die) and (c) (the centre of the die as its centroid; the Lean statements use the origin, and the centroid is not formalized), the finite test for equal masses, and the rest of the paper (the enumeration). Audience: researchers on convex polytopes, the Minkowski and Alexandrov problems and fair dice, and Mathlib contributors.
entries.title: Fair Dice from Curvature: Alexandrov's Theorem, Machine-Checked

entries.abstract: A Lean 4 / Mathlib proof that a finite simple graph G has a total colouring with Δ(G) + 2 colours (a map on V ⊕ E(G) giving different colours to adjacent vertices, to distinct edges with a common endpoint, and to incident vertex–edge pairs) in three situations: (1) tcc_of_independent: G has an independent set S with |V| ≤ |S| + Δ + 1 (Yap–Wang–Zhang 1989, Lemma 2.2; Yap–Chew 1992, Lemma 2.4); (2) tcc_of_card_le_maxDegree_add_three: Δ(G) ≥ |V| − 3 (Yap–Wang–Zhang 1989, Theorem 2.3 and the closing remarks); (3) tcc_of_card_le_maxDegree_add_four: Δ(G) ≥ |V| − 4, for every finite simple graph (no further hypothesis; Yap–Wang–Zhang 1989, Theorem 2.4). The proofs use Yap's apex-vertex technique: a new vertex joined to the vertices outside one or two independent pairs, matchings found by the enlarge-matching argument (when Δ ≥ 7 or G has three pairwise non-adjacent vertices) or, when G has no three pairwise non-adjacent vertices, the two alternating matchings of a Hamiltonian path through the vertices outside the pairs, and Fournier's theorem (PALOMAR-2026-11-08-000009) or Vizing's theorem (PALOMAR-2026-10-15-000004), both imported as lake dependencies, in place of the Chetwynd–Hilton theorem on three vertices of maximum degree and Kostochka's theorem for Δ ≤ 4 used in the original paper.
entries.title: The total colouring conjecture for graphs of high maximum degree (Yap–Wang–Zhang)

entries.abstract: Formalization of the main results of J. Park's paper on stealthy periodic point configurations with marked cubic period 2Zⁿ. From the 24 sign rows of an order-12 Hadamard matrix and their antipodes it constructs, for n = 10, 11, 12, configurations with stealth radius K = 1 and stealth center density 1/24 that are not translates of lattices (Theorem 1.1). It proves that a motif with K ≥ 1 has at least 2n points, with equality for n ≥ 3 exactly for translated antipodal Hadamard arrays (Theorem 1.2); that K > 1 forces at least 1 + n + n(n−1)/2 points (Lemma 4.1); the exact stealth radius of a binary motif in terms of its dual distance (Proposition 3.1); bounded-complexity and binary optimality of the center density 1/(2n), resp. 1/24, with their equality cases (Theorems 5.1 and 5.3, Corollary 5.2); the strict reciprocal-Gram maximum (Lemma 6.1); and local maximality of the Hadamard configurations under perturbations of the motif and of the marked period, with local isolation for n = 12 (Theorem 1.3, in the marked period model).
entries.title: Hadamard configurations and sharp cubic-period bounds for stealth in dimensions 10, 11, and 12

entries.abstract: This is a formalization of Lebesgue space bounds for higher-dimensional twisted paraproducts in the full open Banach range. This was an open problem in every dimension d >= 2. For d = 2, Kovac (Rev. Mat. Iberoam. 2012, Theorem 1) proved bounds for input exponents 1 < p_1, p_2 < infinity with 1/p_1 + 1/p_2 > 1/2, i.e. target exponents p < 2. For d = 3, Durcik and Roos (Proc. AMS 2021, Sections 1 and 3) proved bounds for 1 < p < 4/3 and 1 < p_i < 4. For d >= 4, no bounds were known for any exponents, as stated in Durcik-Roos (2021, Section 1). The proof and the formalization blueprint were generated with GPT-6.2 Astra Ultra. The formalization was done with GPT-6.2 Sol Light.
entries.title: Boundedness of higher-dimensional twisted paraproducts

entries.abstract:
Complete and unconditional. A Lean 4 formalization of G. Cassese, "A solution to Morrey's problem in R^{2 x m}" (arXiv:2608.03488v3, 2026): rank-one convex integrands on 2 x m matrices, m >= 3, that are nowhere quasiconvex, so that with Šverák's theorem only 2 x 2 remains open; and p-homogeneous examples answering Kirchheim and Kristensen's homogeneous problem negatively.

Every result that the paper proves is proved, with no hypothesis beyond the paper's: Theorem 1.2 (every p > 1, 2 x m for m large, by the paper's UMD route, and a second time by its elementary route), Theorem 1.3 (a quartic on 2 x 3, and p near 4), Corollary 5.3 (its transpose on 3 x 2), the consequences that only 2 x 2 remains, Theorem 1.4 (d x d, every p, and p = 4 for d >= 588), Theorem 1.5 (4 x 2, every p != 2) and Corollary 1.6. The results of other works that the proofs use are proved too, in their sources' terms: Burkholder's inequalities and functions, UMD theory for L^p and the Schatten classes, decoupling, the Kahane-Khintchine and non-commutative Khintchine inequalities, transference for homogeneous multipliers, Dragičević's lower bound for the square of the Beurling-Ahlfors transform, Dacorogna's formula for the quasiconvex envelope, Kristensen's smoothing and the textbook facts of the calculus of variations, by the arguments of their sources (named substitutes stand for a few steps that a source takes from a work that was not read, only recalls, or states without proof: see fidelity). They come from three Lake packages written for this project (lean4-harmonic-analysis, lean4-banach-probability, lean4-calculus-of-variations). The repository formalizes other papers on Morrey's problem too, each its own submission.
entries.title: Cassese 2026: Morrey's problem in R^{2 x m}, in Lean

entries.abstract: A Lean 4 formalisation, built on mathlib, of L. Niebel, "Lions' Maximal Regularity Problem for Divergence-Form Differential Operators: Failure at the 1/2-Hölder Endpoint" (arXiv:2608.11194v2), an arXiv preprint. J.-L. Lions asked whether the variational solution of u' + A(t)u = f, u(0) = 0, with forms of bounded measurable coefficients, has maximal L^2-regularity, u' in L^2(0,T;H), when f is in L^2(0,T;H). The paper shows that 1/2-Hölder continuity in time with values in L^infinity does not suffice: on the interval (0,pi) it constructs a bounded, uniformly elliptic, real scalar coefficient, 1/2-Hölder continuous in time with values in L^infinity(0,pi) and arbitrarily close to 1, a continuous L^2-valued forcing, and the unique Lions variational solution, whose time derivative is not square integrable (Theorem 1.1); and, by zero extension, tensorisation and parabolic rescaling, real symmetric isotropic counterexamples on R^d and on every bounded domain of R^d, d >= 1 (Corollary 1.2). The compared theorems are Theorem 1.1 and Corollary 1.2, stated in Challenge.lean in the paper's spaces H = L^2, V = H^1_0 (the closure of the graphs of C^1_c functions) and V' (its anti-dual), with uniqueness of the Lions solution. The repository formalises, in its own terms and with every deviation recorded in DEVIATIONS.md, the other numbered statements of the paper, one of them in part (Corollary 7.1 directly, without the cited sufficiency theorems and the operator-theoretic side conditions), with no counterpart for Remark 3.1 (a comment without a claim), and proves Lions' uniqueness theorem in the paper's complex spaces; about 21,000 lines of Lean in 61 library modules; every theorem of the library depends only on the standard axioms propext, Classical.choice and Quot.sound, and there is no sorry outside the two deliberate ones in Challenge.lean.
entries.title: Lions' maximal regularity problem for divergence-form differential operators: failure at the 1/2-Hölder endpoint

entries.title: Density Hajnal–Szemerédi formalization

entries.abstract:
An infinite Ammann–Beenker network is a mathematical graph with octagonal geometry. In this particular network, two localized wave patterns share a special energy, as established in [PALOMAR-2026-11-06-000012 (version 1)](https://palomar-registry.org/entry?id=PALOMAR-2026-11-06-000012&version=1). [PALOMAR-2026-11-23-000017 (version 1)](https://palomar-registry.org/entry?id=PALOMAR-2026-11-23-000017&version=1) describes how changing a single edge splits their energy. [PALOMAR-2026-11-25-000001 (version 1)](https://palomar-registry.org/entry.html?id=PALOMAR-2026-11-25-000001&version=1) shows how two coordinated controls can prepare any normalized mixture of the two patterns, up to a common phase, without leakage. The present theorem asks whether their energies can also remain separated from all the other energies while those controls are active.

The first control changes a common onsite parameter on eight first-ring vertices by a signed amount δ. The second changes eight distinct inter-ring edges, with no shared endpoints, by a signed amount η. The two localized patterns span a space that both controls preserve exactly. Its two energy levels have midpoint E* + δ/2 + η, where E* is their original common energy, and half-spacing s = √(δ²/4 + η²). Both levels have genuine nonzero eigenvectors of the full infinite operator; they coincide only when both controls vanish. The orthogonal complement is also preserved on the natural operator domain.

At zero control, the certified gap around E* is 1/128. Write ρ = |δ| + 2|η| for the combined control size. The new theorem proves that if ρ/2 + s is less than 1/128, the complete real spectrum contains exactly the two controlled energies in the closed interval between them. Each is separated from every other real spectral energy by at least 1/128 − ρ/2 − s, which is strictly positive. Every eigenvector at either controlled energy lies entirely in the original localized space. The case of coincident energies at zero control is included.

Since s is at most ρ/2, the simpler condition ρ < 1/128 also guarantees protection, with separation at least 1/128 − ρ. This includes either control acting alone, with |δ| < 1/128 or |η| < 1/256, respectively. These bounds are sufficient, not claimed optimal.

The result is proved in Lean for the full infinite operator with its confining potential and natural domain, not for a finite sample or a two-state approximation. It adds a quantitative energy gap to exact geometric decoupling. It provides a foundation for studying imperfect controls, but does not prove noise tolerance, arbitrary-strength protection, experimental feasibility or general quantum dynamics.
entries.title: Spectral Protection During Coordinated Control on an Infinite Ammann–Beenker Graph

entries.abstract: Let b(n, l) be the number of parking functions of length n whose maximum displacement is exactly l, where the displacement of a car is the distance between the spot it takes and its preferred spot, and call the sequence b(n, 0), b(n, 1), ..., b(n, n-1) row n. The formalization proves two theorems in Lean 4 with Mathlib. The first, the staircase (Parking.staircase), says that for every n >= 2 there is a position p such that row n rises strictly up to b(n, p), satisfies b(n, p+1) <= b(n, p), and falls strictly from b(n, p+1) on, and such that row n+1 either has the same shape with the same p or rises strictly up to b(n+1, p+1) and falls strictly after it. So every row is strictly increasing and then strictly decreasing, except that the entry directly after the peak may be equal to the peak, and the peak stays or moves one position to the right when the length grows by one. The second (Parking.unimodal_via_staircase) is the corollary that for every n >= 1 row n is unimodal, which is Conjecture 6.5 of Celano, Elder, Hadaway, Harris, Martin, Priestley and Udell (arXiv:2507.07243). The numbers b(n, l) are defined directly from the parking process. The staircase is obtained by induction on n from two rules for the sign of the step b(n, k) - b(n, k-1): a positive step stays positive one row down in the same column, and a step that is not positive is followed by a negative step one row down and one column to the right. The rules are proved region by region: tables that Lean's kernel evaluates in exact integer arithmetic settle the small columns, and analytic estimates settle the large ones. The proof depends only on the axioms propext, Classical.choice and Quot.sound. The unimodality had been proved before, by another route, in the formalization MegasKomnenos/parking-unimodality (PALOMAR-2026-11-25-000002), on whose library this proof is built. As far as a literature search found, the staircase is first presented by this formalization and the package from which it was made; that it is new is not established. The proof was found, written and formalized by AI sessions. A person has read the two Lean statements, with the definitions they use, against the statements in words; no person has refereed the mathematics.
entries.title: The staircase theorem for parking functions counted by maximum displacement

entries.abstract: A Mathlib-only Lean 4 formalization of the manuscript Characterizations of E-finite algebras and conjectures on brick-finiteness by Haruhisa Enomoto. A finite-dimensional algebra over a field is E-finite when its two-term silting fan covers the integral projective lattice K₀(proj Λ). Theorem A proves that E-finiteness is equivalent over an arbitrary field to seventeen conditions—including nonzero morphisms between nonzero modules of equal dimension vector (K₀-Hom), injectivity of dimension-vector maps on torsion-class Grothendieck monoids, functorial finiteness of compact torsion classes and wide subcategories, finiteness of semibricks, finiteness of bricks of each endolength, polynomial brick growth, absence of generic bricks and generic grains, presilting generation of two-term thick subcategories, and finite-dimensionality of universal localizations and simple Artinian epimorphic targets—together with two dimension-vector finiteness conditions over infinite fields and three geometric conditions (King moduli closed points, open brick orbits, and open wide loci) over algebraically closed fields. Consequently, seven open brick-finiteness conjectures (including Demonet's lattice point conjecture, the finite semibrick conjecture, the second brick-Brauer–Thrall conjecture, and Mousavand–Paquette's generic brick conjecture) become equivalent for each algebra. Theorem B proves this common conjecture in rank at most two over any field, equating E-finiteness, brick-finiteness, and τ-tilting finiteness. Corollary C proves Weyman's conjecture over algebraically closed fields of arbitrary characteristic, equating Schur-representation-finiteness with multiplicity-freeness on every irreducible component. Intended for researchers in the representation theory of finite-dimensional algebras, silting and τ-tilting theory, and module varieties.
entries.title: Characterizations of E-finite algebras and conjectures on brick-finiteness

entries.abstract: A machine-checked proof of the Eastin-Knill theorem: a quantum code of dimension at least two that detects every error on a single subsystem has no universal set of transversal logical gates. The system has finitely many sites of any finite dimensions; a code is an orthogonal projector P; it detects single-site errors when P E P is a multiple of P for every operator E on one site; a transversal gate is a tensor product of one unitary per site, and it is logical when it commutes with P. Up to a scalar on the code there are only finitely many logical transversal gates; if the code has dimension at least two they are not universal, since some logical unitary differs on the code by a fixed distance from every logical transversal gate times every scalar. The same holds for transversal gates across several code blocks (Eastin and Knill's Corollary 1). The proof avoids Lie theory: near the identity a transversal gate is exp(i H) with H a sum of single-site operators, error detection makes it act on the code as a scalar, so the gates acting as scalars form an open subgroup of a compact group, which has finite index. A three-qutrit code is constructed to show the hypotheses can be met.
entries.title: The Eastin-Knill theorem

entries.abstract: A Lean 4 / Mathlib proof of the main results of Fan, Stone, Yang and Yin, "Localization-delocalization transition for a random block matrix model" (arXiv:2504.00512). The model is H_Lambda = H + Lambda, complex Hermitian case: H has D >= 2 independent N x N Wigner blocks on the diagonal, with entry laws whose moments are bounded by given constants (Assumption 1), and Lambda places a deterministic A and A* on the cyclic off-diagonal blocks. This entry contains Theorem 2.1 (delocalized regime: under ||A|| <= N^{-delta_A} and (2.4), every eigenvector puts mass 1/D + O(N^{-c}) on each block, (2.5)) and Theorem 2.5 (localized regime: the eigenvalue shift bounds (2.10), (2.11) and the comparison of the local correlation functions with those of H). Both are stated in uniform form (constants chosen before N, then every N >= N_0, every entry law with the given moment constants, every admissible A and every k) and have no hypotheses other than their parameters; no result of another work is assumed for them. The library also proves Theorem 2.2 and Theorem 2.4, each from one external input stated as an explicit hypothesis; those two are not part of this entry.
entries.title: Localization-delocalization transition for a random block matrix model

entries.abstract: There is a countable group that is hyperlinear and not sofic. This answers in the negative Open question 3.4 of Pestov's guide to hyperlinear and sofic groups (2008): "Is every hyperlinear group sofic?" Soficity and hyperlinearity are stated through finite models: maps to the permutations of a finite set, respectively to unitary matrices, that are multiplicative on a given finite set up to epsilon and separate its elements by 1 - epsilon in normalized Hamming distance, respectively by 2 - epsilon in squared normalized Hilbert-Schmidt distance. The development proves that the first notion is equivalent to the criterion of Pestov's Theorem 3.5 and that the second implies the criterion of his Theorem 3.6. The group is the quotient of GL_3(A) x| St by the subgroup generated by a central element of infinite order, where A is a ring that is free of rank 8 over Z[1/2] with a nilpotent ideal of rank 7, and St is the stabilizer of a vector in GL_3(Z[1/2]). Hyperlinearity of such a central quotient is an instance of a theorem of Thom (2010) and is proved here directly. The non-soficity is the new part: the image of EL_3(A) has Kazhdan's property (T), and eight elements normalizing it act on three of its central elements in a way that no sofic approximation can follow. The proof reuses the Lean developments of OpenAI (Kun's theorem on sofic approximations of Kazhdan groups, cluster groups) and of the group-approximation project (the theorem of Ershov and Jaikin-Zapirain). This formalization does not certify finite generation or finite presentation of the group, the equivalence of the local criteria with the ultraproduct definitions, or anything about other groups.
entries.title: A countable group that is hyperlinear and not sofic

entries.abstract: A Lean 4 proof of Theorem 1.1 of van den Brand, Chen, Kyng, Liu, Peng, Probst Gutenberg, Sachdeva and Sidford: there is a deterministic algorithm that, given a graph with m edges, integral demands and capacities bounded by U and integral costs bounded by C, computes an exact minimum-cost flow in time m^(1+o(1)) log U log C. The algorithm is one program for a word RAM, and the proof shows that on every well-formed instance it halts with a correct answer within K*n + (m+2)^(1+eps(m)) * log(U+2) * log(C+2) steps, with eps(m) tending to 0. Every cited result that the paper uses is proved in the library, or replaced by a proof of the step that uses it.
entries.title: Deterministic almost-linear-time minimum-cost flow

entries.abstract: Lean 4 (v4.35.0) + Mathlib formalization of the base-b last-digit Collatz family f_b(n) = n/2 (even n) and (n mod b)*n + 1 (odd n), focusing on the base-10 Ouroboros map f = f_10 and stating the open OuroborosConjecture definition alongside 38 unconditionally proved compared theorems (zero sorry, zero native_decide, standard axioms only). Collectively, the 38 theorems establish six principal result families: (1) small-base resolutions, including base-4 equivalence to the classical 3x+1 Collatz conjecture and global convergence to 1 in bases 2 and 5; (2) base-10 exponential Terras stopping-time descent (p_k <= 1.124953 * 0.996423^k) and density-one descent, together with a complete all-even-base stopping-time dichotomy (p_infty(b) = 0 iff b in {2, 4, 6, 10}) and even-base drift classification; (3) the base-10 basin-of-1 modulo-30 residue law, exact 2-adic Cantor closure and ultrametric isometry, and exact Hausdorff and box-counting dimension dim_H = dim_B = beta = -log_2 a (plus congruence-class completions and exact base-b suffix-closure dimension in every base b >= 2); (4) sharp pure-kernel basin growth bounds (0.0145 X^(399/800) <= N_1(X) <= C X^0.6245 with limsup (log N_1 / log X) <= 0.6245 < beta, N_5(X) > 0.02134 X^(13/20), and strict separation N_1(X)/N_5(X) <= C X^(-0.0255) -> 0); (5) universal odd-base Markov absorption for all odd b >= 3 and a certified 905/999 odd-base survey through b <= 1999 (27 trap-only and 878 split rational densities, plus explicit b = 3, 5, 7, 13 evaluations); and (6) base-10 cycle obstructions (digit-cancellation, halving-budget, K > 64000 tail, and unconditional classification of all cycles with m <= 3 odd members alongside the two known cycles through 1 and 5). Main results in the companion paper: 15 of 16 proved main results in Lean 4 (94%) · 1 of 16 by external computation (exhaustive sweep and cycle lower bounds through 10^15) · 0 by written proof · Global conjecture open. Within this package, 19 library modules in Ouroboros/ (plus Challenge.lean and Solution.lean) import Mathlib directly while the 104 finite certificate shards (BasinFiveCert*, EvenBasesCert, BasinOneLowerCert*, BasinOneUpperCert*, and OddSurveyCert*) verify finite integer inequalities by Init-only kernel reduction (rfl). Companion working paper, exact external checkers, and logged prior-work searches are published at https://mathdiscoveries.org/results/the-ouroboros-conjecture.html.
entries.title: The Ouroboros Conjecture: Competing Attractors in Base 10 Among Last-Digit Collatz Maps

entries.abstract: DICTO's paper "From Dehn Packets to Scutoids: How the Fullerene Star Fills Space" (Zenodo, 2026) proves, as its Theorem 4, that two pairs of icosahedral pieces whose Dehn invariants cancel cannot tile space: (a) no tiling of 3-space contains a dodecahedron centre pyramid or a truncated icosahedron if every tile is a similar copy (motion, reflection, positive scaling) of one of these two, of the dodecahedron, the icosahedron, the truncated octahedron or the truncated cuboctahedron, or a convex polytope whose dihedral angles are all nonnegative rational multiples of pi; (b) the same for the icosahedron centre pyramid and the truncated dodecahedron. The tiling need not be face to face. This entry proves (a) and (b) in Lean, with each named solid given by exact face inequalities over Q(sqrt 5) or Q(sqrt 2) and its dihedral angles read from the set itself, as in the registered Dehn Canon entry: at an edge point, the share of a small disc across the edge that lies in the tangent cone. It also proves the paper's two lemmas: Lemma 3, that pi, arctan(phi), arccos(1/sqrt 6) and arccos(sqrt(2/3)) are linearly independent over Q (Niven's theorem in Mathlib and a field argument), and Lemma 2 in the weaker form the proof of Theorem 4 needs: at an edge point x of a tile of a tiling by convex polytopes (locally finite, not necessarily face to face) there are finitely many tiles with numbers summing to 2 pi, the given tile's being its angle at x and each other being pi, 2 pi, or a dihedral angle of that tile read at some edge point of it, chosen independently and not necessarily on the given edge. The paper takes Lemma 2 from DICTO's earlier paper "Aristotle's Pyramid"; it is the edge-counting step behind Debrunner's theorem (1980). The proof of Theorem 4 counts the angles round one edge: the coefficients of the three irrational angles must cancel within one turn, and a weight argument removes the pieces one after another. All the paper's helpers are covered, the truncated icosidodecahedron included, each built from exact coordinates. Not formalized in the Challenge: Theorem 4 (c), on the smallest ring, is proved in the library but is not in the Challenge; the rest of the paper (scutoid fillings, the Fullerene Star). Audience: researchers on tilings, space-filling polyhedra and scissors congruence, and Mathlib contributors.
entries.title: Dehn Packets in Lean: two icosahedral pairs that cannot fill space

entries.abstract: Lean 4 (v4.35.0) + Mathlib formalization of structural theorems, edge-dual linear-programming relaxations (Lemma W and refinements), Lemma C, local obstruction rules, unconditional counterexample lower bounds, explicit ceiling witnesses, and conditional transfer theorems for Giuga's conjecture (1950). Across 21 compared theorems (zero sorry, zero native_decide, standard axioms only), Lean 4 proves unconditionally that every Giuga counterexample has at least 578 distinct prime factors and exceeds 10^1803 (at least 1,804 decimal digits), constructs an explicit 8,135-prime normal odd prime set (40,733 digits) and an explicit 8,138-prime witness satisfying all seven local counterexample rules (40,751 digits), proves all forms of Lemma W, Lemma C, and the mod-8 count congruence, and proves conditional lifting theorems reaching >= 8,138 prime factors and > 10^40747 (>= 40,748 decimal digits) from explicit depth-6 frontier hypotheses. Main results in the companion paper: 0 of 2 headline theorems purely in Lean 4 (0%) · 2 of 2 by Lean 4 + external exact-integer certificates (all 15 prefixes below 17). Existence of a Giuga counterexample remains open. Companion working paper, exact integer checker, and prior-work search log: https://mathdiscoveries.org/results/giuga.
entries.title: How Many Prime Factors Could a Counterexample to Giuga's Conjecture Have?

entries.abstract: At every sufficiently large order n, we construct a split graph with an integral–fractional clique-partition gap of order at least (pn)^(3/2). If p^2 n exceeds an explicit constant times log n, independent survival of crossing edges with probability p leaves, with probability at least 1 - 2 n^(-8), both a complete physical reassignment and the same gap. The accompanying bipartite lemma explicitly chooses each host from its own surviving list.
entries.title: Physical host recovery and gap preservation after random crossing-edge deletions

entries.abstract: A Lean 4 and Mathlib formalization of maximum flows and shortest paths. Plane graphs are combinatorial maps (darts with a reversal, a tail vertex, a face and a next dart along the face boundary) whose graph and dual are connected and which satisfy Euler's formula |V| + |F| = |D|/2 + 2. The machine statements are about one explicit word RAM (unit cost per instruction, natural registers and memory cells bounded by a word bound W along the run) and fixed encodings of the inputs as lists of natural numbers; each asserts one fixed word program for all inputs (the machine also has exact real registers, and a word program contains no instruction that uses them). Six theorems are compared: (1) the max-flow min-cut theorem for a network with nonnegative integer capacities and disjoint sets of sources and sinks: some flow and some cut have equal value and capacity, so the flow is maximum and the cut minimum; (2) the theorem of Miller and Naor: on a plane map, given an antisymmetric g with net outflow b at every vertex, a b-flow within the capacities u exists if and only if the dual graph with lengths u - g has a feasible potential; (3) a word program decides, for every well-formed encoding of a plane map with V vertices, F faces and S darts, natural capacities, supplies and demands, whether a feasible flow exists, within 26 (S + 2)(V + F + 2) steps; (4) a word program prints, for each vertex of a digraph with n vertices, m arcs and natural lengths, its distance from a source capped at a given value INF (so INF for unreachable vertices), within (n + m + 1)(36 floor(log2 n) + 143) steps; (5) a word program prints the size of a maximum matching of a bipartite graph with n vertices and m arcs within 80 (n + 1)(n + m + 1) steps; (6) there are a word program and constants c and k such that, for every well-formed encoding of a plane map (loops allowed) with n darts, K vertices, natural capacities and disjoint sets of sources and sinks, and every word bound W >= c (7 s)^k, where s is n + K plus the total capacity plus 2, the program prints a maximum flow from the sources to the sinks, as a table of flow values together with a valid index into it for every dart, within c (n + K + 1)(floor(log2 n) + 1)^3 steps; this is the algorithm of Borradaile, Klein, Mozes, Nussbaum and Wulff-Nilsen. The proofs use only the axioms propext, Classical.choice and Quot.sound.
entries.title: Flows and shortest paths in plane graphs, with machine programs including the maximum-flow algorithm of Borradaile, Klein, Mozes, Nussbaum and Wulff-Nilsen, in Lean 4
